# Finding and downloading bursts

A search asks the CDSE catalog which bursts exist for a place and a time
window, and a download fetches them. Searching needs no account and downloads
nothing, so you can refine a query freely before committing to a download.

## Search an area

Pass an area of interest as a shapely geometry in longitude and latitude,
together with a time window. The search returns every burst that overlaps the
area and shows their footprints on a map:

```{python}
from shapely.geometry import box
from s1bursts import BurstCatalog, FileManager, SearchQuery, TimeRange

catalog = BurstCatalog(FileManager("data"))
bursts = catalog.search(SearchQuery(
    intersects=box(8.00, 46.40, 8.08, 46.48),
    time_range=TimeRange("2022-01-01", "2022-01-31"),
    polarization="VV",
))
bursts
```

Even a small area usually returns several footprints. Bursts from different
orbits and sub-swaths overlap the same few kilometers, each seeing the ground
from a different direction. The area selects whole bursts and does not crop
them. A `TimeRange` covers whole days, and both end dates are included.

## Follow one footprint

To follow one footprint through time, search by `burst_id` and `sub_swath`
instead of by area. This is the usual query once an area search has shown which
footprint covers your site best:

```{.python}
bursts = catalog.search(SearchQuery(
    time_range=TimeRange("2022-01-01", "2022-12-31"),
    burst_id=30346, sub_swath="IW1", polarization="VV",
))
```

`SearchQuery` also filters by orbit, pass direction and acquisition mode; its
[reference](../reference/query.SearchQuery.qmd) lists every field.

::: {.callout-note}
A search returns every matching burst, up to 1000, the size of one catalog
page. A query that matches more raises `TooManyResultsError` rather than return
an incomplete list. Narrow the time window or the area, or split the query and
[combine the results](#combine-searches).
:::

## Combine searches

Search results add up with `+`, which drops any duplicates. Use this to collect
several searches into one download, for example the same footprint in winter
and in summer:

```{python}
footprint = dict(burst_id=30346, sub_swath="IW1", polarization="VV")
winter = catalog.search(SearchQuery(time_range=TimeRange("2022-01-01", "2022-01-31"), **footprint))
summer = catalog.search(SearchQuery(time_range=TimeRange("2022-07-01", "2022-07-31"), **footprint))
both = winter + summer
print(len(winter), len(summer), len(both))
```

## Select part of a search

A search result can be narrowed without a new query. Each selection returns a
new collection, so they can be chained:

| Method | Keeps the bursts |
|---|---|
| `within(time_range)` | Acquired on a day of a `TimeRange` |
| `intersecting(geometry)` | Whose footprint touches a geometry, such as an area or an [MGRS grid square](compositing.qmd#get-the-grid-squares) |
| `filter(**fields)` | Whose fields equal a value, or any value of a list |

```{.python}
january = bursts.within(TimeRange("2022-01-01", "2022-01-31"))
descending = bursts.filter(pass_direction="Descending", rel_orbit_number=[66, 139])
```

## Pair acquisitions

Coherence compares two acquisitions of the same footprint. `find_pairs()` turns
a search result into pairs a fixed number of days apart, which can be
downloaded and [processed](processing.qmd#coherence) like single bursts:

```{.python}
pairs = bursts.find_pairs(baseline=12)
```

The baseline is a whole number of days, and both arguments are passed by
keyword. `max_delta` sets how far the actual spacing may deviate from it, six
hours by default. A pair needs both of its acquisitions, so search a little
beyond the end of the period you want and keep the pairs that start within
it:

```{.python}
pairs = bursts.find_pairs(baseline=12).starting_within(january)
```

## Save a search

Save a search result if you want to rerun an analysis on exactly the same
acquisitions later. The records live in a GeoDataFrame, which can be written to
GeoParquet and loaded again without querying the catalog:

```{.python}
import geopandas as gpd
from s1bursts.burst import BurstCollection

bursts.df.to_parquet("inventory.parquet")
bursts = BurstCollection(gpd.read_parquet("inventory.parquet"))
```

## Download the bursts

`BurstCatalog.download()` fetches the bursts of a search result, or both
acquisitions of every pair. Bursts already on disk are skipped, so an
interrupted download can be run again:

```{.python}
summary = catalog.download(bursts, max_workers=4)
summary.print_summary()
```

`max_workers` sets how many bursts download in parallel. Each file lands in the
`s1-slc` folder below the `FileManager`'s base directory.

## When the burst service fails

CDSE's burst service occasionally fails for particular bursts. If
[CDSE S3 keys](environment-variables.qmd#cdse-credentials) are set, s1bursts
then extracts the burst from the full scene on CDSE's S3 storage instead. This
route is slower but usually succeeds. Without the keys, the burst is recorded as
failed. Pass `endpoint="s3"` to try the S3 route first.

## Failed downloads

A failed burst does not stop the download by default. It is recorded in the
returned `OperationSummary` and the remaining bursts continue. Check the
summary before processing: `raise_on_failure()` raises an
`OperationFailedError` that lists every failed burst, and otherwise returns the
summary, so it can follow the call directly:

```{.python}
catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure()
```

To inspect the failures yourself, read them from the summary:

```{.python}
for failure in summary.failed_items:
    print(failure.source.date, failure.error)
```

Most failures are temporary server errors and succeed on a second run, which
downloads only the missing bursts. To stop at the first failure instead,
create the catalog with `BurstCatalog(fm, continue_on_error=False)`. A burst
that CDSE reports as missing is not requested again by the same
`BurstCatalog`; create a new one to retry it later. To accept such bursts and
continue, ignore their error type:

```{.python}
from s1bursts.errors import BurstNotFoundError

catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure(ignore=BurstNotFoundError)
```

## Reuse downloaded bursts

`FileManager` lists what is already stored, without a new search. Use this to
process bursts downloaded in an earlier session:

```{.python}
from s1bursts import FileManager
from s1bursts.burst import Burst

fm = FileManager("data")
bursts = fm.find(Burst, burst_id=30346, time_range=TimeRange("2022-01-01", "2022-06-30"))
```

The result is a list of bursts, which the processing methods accept as it is.
To [form pairs](#pair-acquisitions), turn it into a collection first with
`BurstCollection.from_bursts(bursts)`.

`find()` lists every product and composite type the same way: pass the type,
such as `RTCProduct` or `RTCLRWComposite` from `s1bursts.product`, and filter
on the fields its filename records. These listings are rebuilt from filenames,
so they hold less information than the original search result;
[save the search](#save-a-search) if you need the full catalog record.

### The burst-ID map

A burst from a search carries its relative orbit, pass direction and footprint,
and product and SLC filenames record the orbit and pass direction, so the usual
search, download, process and composite workflow needs no further data. Only a
burst that did not come from a search needs to look these up, in the
[burst-ID map](https://sar-mpc.eu/sar-mpc-products/) published by SAR-MPC.
That applies to a burst you construct by hand, and to the footprint of a burst
found with `find(Burst)`, which its filename does not record. Download the map
once, about 500 MB per acquisition mode, when you need it:

```{.python}
from s1bursts import download_burst_map

download_burst_map(mode="IW")
```
